newsitem.title: CHINA: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - IFCT makes comeback.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - IFCT makes comeback.

text.p: Two months after credit fears prompted it to abort an issue, Industrial Finance Corp of Thailand (IFCT) has structured a debt issue with "credit" clauses to calm nervous investors.
IFCT issued a US$250 million five-year bond at 120 basis points over U.S. Treasuries, and a US$250 million 10-year tranche at 112.5 basis points over, featuring a five-year put at par.
The issue attracted interest for two major reasons: it was the first significant international Thai deal since the Thai baht hit a wall, and, second, it contained a credit clause.
While not as big a success as the global issue by Hutchison Whampoa Ltd, also rated A3, it attracted about US$1 billion in bids, said a source at Lehman Brothers, which arranged the issue for IFCT.

"Both the 10-year (with put at five) and the straight five have, basically, provisions embedded in them that stipulate that if the credit of IFCT is downgraded the coupon will step up," said a source at Lehman Brothers.
"If either S&P (Standard & Poor's) or Moody's (Investor Service) downgrades them by two notches, then the coupon will step up 50 basis points," he said.
"It's 25 basis points per notch thereafter," he said.
It also included a put option allowing investors to put the paper back to IFCT if its rating fell below investment grade.
The source said IFCT's pricing was in line with that on its outstanding debt in the secondary market.
Credit clauses are seen as a way for issuers to allay investor fears of downgrades, and return to international markets despite continuing credit or currency concerns, bankers said.

"It reflects increased concern about some of these markets," said one fixed income analyst, referring particularly to Korea and Thailand, both big U.S. issuers but both suffering from either credit or currency related problems.
The Kingdom of Thailand paid a spread of 90 basis points over Treasuries for a US$600 million 10-year issue in April.
IFCT, an early victim of investor jitters about Thailand, pulled a US$50 million step-up floating-rate note (FRN) in June, just days after its launch after being downgraded.

Bankers said credit clauses might be a way for Asians to refinance at low rates through the U.S. market, but warned that issuers would have to be sure about their rating outlook before locking in punitive credit clauses.
The issue provided welcome interest in a market that remains lacklustre, partly because many bankers are holidaying, but also because currency concerns have cooled local debt issuers' ardour.
In other news, Fujian International Trust and Investment Corporation (FITIC) has received a BBB rating from S&P for a forthcoming US$100 million 10-year Yankee issue.
